SELLER'S PERMIT (CALIFORNIA DEPARTMENT OF TAX AND FEE ADMINISTRATION REGISTRATION) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Retail, LLC · limited liability company

SELLER'S PERMIT INFORMATION SHEET — PURPOSE AND SCOPE
This information sheet relates to Acme Retail, LLC, a limited liability company, with a California place of business at 100 Market Street, San Diego, CA, engaged in selling retail clothing and accessories. It describes California's statutory requirement, set out in the Sales and Use Tax Law (Revenue and Taxation Code Division 2, Part 1), that a person desiring to engage in business as a seller of tangible personal property in California register with the California Department of Tax and Fee Administration (CDTFA) and hold a seller's permit for each place of business, along with the statutory definitions that determine who that requirement reaches, how a permit is issued and may be suspended or revoked, the criminal penalty for engaging in business as a seller without one, and CDTFA's statutory authority to require a security deposit. This document is not this project's LLC Articles of Organization, Articles of Incorporation, Statement of Information, Fictitious Business Name (DBA) Statement, or Foreign LLC/Corporation Qualification document. Those documents concern filings with the California Secretary of State: creating a corporation or LLC, that entity's periodic reporting after formation, county-level registration of a name other than a registrant's true legal name, or an out-of-state entity's registration to transact business in California. This document instead concerns a separate statutory scheme administered by a separate state agency — CDTFA's registration of retail sellers under the Sales and Use Tax Law — which applies regardless of how, or whether, the seller's business is formed or named, and applies independently of any Secretary of State filing. A business can complete every Business Formation filing in this project and still separately need to register with CDTFA, and a person can need to register with CDTFA without forming any entity at all. This information sheet is educational only. It does not itself register Acme Retail, LLC, or any other person, with CDTFA; it does not determine whether Acme Retail, LLC's specific activities constitute engaging in business as a seller within the meaning of California law; and it does not obtain a seller's permit for Acme Retail, LLC or any other person.

REQUIREMENT TO FILE AN APPLICATION FOR A SELLER'S PERMIT
California's Sales and Use Tax Law states that every person desiring to engage in or conduct business as a seller within California shall file an application for a permit for each place of business. The application must be made on a form the agency prescribes, must state the name under which the applicant transacts or intends to transact business and the location of the applicant's place or places of business, must state that the applicant will actively engage in or conduct business as a seller of tangible personal property, and may be filed using electronic media. The statute itself directs this filing to "the board," a reference to the former State Board of Equalization's sales and use tax function. Since July 1, 2017, California's Government Code states that the California Department of Tax and Fee Administration (CDTFA) is the successor to, and is vested with, all of the duties, powers, and responsibilities the board held under sales and use tax statutes such as this one; CDTFA is accordingly the agency that now administers the seller's-permit application requirement described here, even though the codified text of Section 6066 has not been amended to replace the word "board" with "department."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Every person desiring to engage in or conduct business as a seller within this state shall file with the board an application for a permit for each place of business. Every application for a permit shall be made upon a form prescribed by the board and shall set forth the name under which the applicant transacts or intends to transact business, the location of his place or places of business, and such other information as the board may require."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax Code § 6066(a), California Sales and Use Tax Law, Article 2 (Permits), application requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=6066.)
  "the department is the successor to, and is vested with, all of the duties, powers, and responsibilities of the board."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 15570.22, Government Code, transfer of the State Board of Equalization's sales and use tax duties to CDTFA (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=15570.22.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own seller's-permit filing requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific person's obligations, and not a claim that other states impose an identical registration requirement for retail sellers. This clause cites a single subsection of one Revenue and Taxation Code section, Section 6066(a), together with a section of a different code, Government Code Section 15570.22, for the separate point that CDTFA succeeded to the former State Board of Equalization's sales-tax duties; these are two independent sources on two different points, not multiple subsections of the same section presented as corroborating each other. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself file an application for a seller's permit with CDTFA on behalf of the business named in this document or any other person, and it does not determine whether any specific person is required to hold one.

STATUTORY DEFINITIONS OF "SELLER" AND "RETAILER"
The seller's-permit filing requirement applies to a person engaging in business "as a seller," a term the Sales and Use Tax Law defines separately from "retailer." "Seller" includes every person engaged in the business of selling tangible personal property of a kind whose gross receipts from a retail sale are required to be included in the measure of the sales tax, whether or not that particular property is ever actually sold at retail. "Retailer" is defined separately and more narrowly, and includes every seller who makes any retail sale of tangible personal property, every person engaged in the business of making retail sales at auction of tangible personal property owned by that person or others, and every person engaged in the business of making sales for storage, use, or other consumption. The statute also lets the state tax agency treat certain salespersons, representatives, peddlers, or canvassers as agents of the dealers, distributors, or employers they sell for, and separately provides that a newspaper carrier is not a retailer.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "“Seller” includes every person engaged in the business of selling tangible personal property of a kind the gross receipts from the retail sale of which are required to be included in the measure of the sales tax."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax Code § 6014, California Sales and Use Tax Law, Chapter 1 (General Provisions and Definitions), definition of "seller" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=6014.)
  "“Retailer” includes: (1) Every seller who makes any retail sale or sales of tangible personal property, and every person engaged in the business of making retail sales at auction of tangible personal property owned by the person or others."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax Code § 6015(a)(1), California Sales and Use Tax Law, Chapter 1 (General Provisions and Definitions), definition of "retailer" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=6015.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California defines "seller" and "retailer" for its own sales and use tax law — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific person's activities, and not a claim that other states define these terms identically. This clause cites two different statutory sections, not subsections of one section: Cal. Rev. & Tax Code § 6014 defines "seller," and Cal. Rev. & Tax Code § 6015(a)(1) defines "retailer," in separately worded provisions; these are treated as two independent sources on two related but distinct terms, not as one term's definition standing in for the other. This information sheet is informational only: it does not determine whether the business named in this document or any other specific person is a "seller" or "retailer" within the meaning of California law.

STATUTORY DEFINITIONS OF "SALE" AND "RETAIL SALE"
The permit requirement is further keyed to what counts as a "sale" and a "retail sale." As currently operative, "sale" means and includes any transfer of title or possession, exchange, or barter, conditional or otherwise, in any manner or by any means whatsoever, of tangible personal property for a consideration, among several other enumerated transactions (including certain fabrication and processing work, and most leases of tangible personal property) that the same section separately treats as sales. A "retail sale" or "sale at retail" is defined separately, in a different section, as a sale for a purpose other than resale in the regular course of business, in the form of tangible personal property, with a further provision extending that definition to a sale by a convicted counterfeiter regardless of resale purpose.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "“Sale” means and includes: (a) Any transfer of title or possession, exchange, or barter, conditional or otherwise, in any manner or by any means whatsoever, of tangible personal property for a consideration."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax Code § 6006, California Sales and Use Tax Law, Chapter 1 (General Provisions and Definitions), definition of "sale" (version operative through December 31, 2026) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=6006.)
  "A “retail sale” or “sale at retail” means a sale for a purpose other than resale in the regular course of business in the form of tangible personal property."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax Code § 6007(a)(1), California Sales and Use Tax Law, Chapter 1 (General Provisions and Definitions), definition of "retail sale"/"sale at retail" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=6007.)

This clause cites two different statutory sections, not subsections of one section: Cal. Rev. & Tax Code § 6006 defines "sale," and Cal. Rev. & Tax Code § 6007(a)(1) defines "retail sale"/"sale at retail," in separately worded provisions, treated as two independent sources on two related but distinct terms. Section 6006 has already been amended by Statutes 2026, Chapter 23 to add digital-product provisions and to rename the administering agency in its text from "the board" to "the department," but that amendment does not become operative until January 1, 2027; the text quoted here is the version that was operative on the checkedDate above, and this clause does not describe the version taking effect January 1, 2027. This information sheet is informational only: it does not determine whether any specific transaction of the business named in this document or any other person is a "sale" or "retail sale" within the meaning of California law.

ISSUANCE OF THE PERMIT AND ITS NON-ASSIGNABILITY
Once an applicant has complied with the application requirement of Section 6066 and, where applicable, the security requirement of Section 6701, and after the applicant has been given the notice Section 6066.5 requires, California's Sales and Use Tax Law directs the state tax agency to grant and issue to each applicant a separate permit for each place of business within the state. The statute states that a permit is not assignable and is valid only for the person in whose name it is issued and for the transaction of business at the place designated in it, and that it must at all times be conspicuously displayed at the place for which it was issued.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "the board shall grant and issue to each applicant a separate permit for each place of business within the state. A permit is not assignable and is valid only for the person in whose name it is issued and for the transaction of business at the place designated therein. It shall at all times be conspicuously displayed at the place for which issued."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax Code § 6067, California Sales and Use Tax Law, Article 2 (Permits), issuance and non-assignability (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=6067.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own rule that a seller's permit is non-assignable and place- and person-specific — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific permit, and not a claim that other states' analogous licenses are non-transferable in the same way. This clause quotes a single statutory section, Cal. Rev. & Tax Code § 6067, so no same-section multiple-subsection issue arises here. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself issue a seller's permit to the business named in this document or any other person, and it does not determine whether any specific person or place of business qualifies for one.

SUSPENSION OR REVOCATION OF A SELLER'S PERMIT
None of the seller's-permit statutes reviewed for this document set a fixed expiration date or a recurring renewal period for a permit once issued. California's Sales and Use Tax Law instead addresses how a permit may end before its holder ends the underlying business: whenever a person fails to comply with any Sales Tax Law provision or related regulation, the state tax agency, after giving the person 10 days' written notice of a hearing and requiring the person to show cause why the permit or permits should not be revoked, may revoke or suspend any one or more of that person's permits following the hearing. The agency must give the permit holder written notice of any suspension or revocation, and the statute separately restricts reissuance: the agency may not issue a new permit after a revocation unless it is satisfied the former holder will comply with the Sales Tax Law and its regulations going forward.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Whenever any person fails to comply with any provision of this part relating to the sales tax or any rule or regulation of the board relating to the sales tax prescribed and adopted under this part, the board upon hearing, after giving the person 10 days’ notice in writing specifying the time and place of hearing and requiring him to show cause why his permit or permits should not be revoked, may revoke or suspend any one or more of the permits held by the person."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax Code § 6070, California Sales and Use Tax Law, Article 2 (Permits), suspension and revocation procedure (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=6070.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own suspension-and-revocation procedure for seller's permits — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific permit, and not a claim that other states use an identical hearing procedure or notice period. This clause quotes a single statutory section, Cal. Rev. & Tax Code § 6070, so no same-section multiple-subsection issue arises here. This information sheet is informational only: it does not determine whether any specific person's permit has been or should be suspended or revoked, and it does not itself provide the notice, conduct the hearing, or take any action this statute describes.

CRIMINAL PENALTY FOR ENGAGING IN BUSINESS AS A SELLER WITHOUT A PERMIT
California's Sales and Use Tax Law makes it a misdemeanor for a person to engage in business as a seller in California without a permit or permits, or to continue doing so after a permit has been suspended or revoked; the statute extends this to each officer of a corporation that engages in business as a seller without a permit. Rather than stating its own fine amount, Section 6071 cross-references Section 7153, the Sales and Use Tax Law's general misdemeanor-penalty provision. Section 7153 states that a violation of the Sales and Use Tax Law, except as otherwise provided, is a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of not less than $1,000 and not more than $5,000, or by imprisonment not exceeding one year in county jail, or by both the fine and imprisonment, in the court's discretion.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A person who engages in business as a seller in this state without a permit or permits or after a permit has been suspended or revoked, and each officer of any corporation which so engages in business, is guilty of a misdemeanor punishable as provided in Section 7153."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax Code § 6071, California Sales and Use Tax Law, Article 2 (Permits), misdemeanor for unlicensed selling (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=6071.)
  "Any violation of this part by any person, except as otherwise provided, is a misdemeanor. Each offense shall be punished by a fine of not less than one thousand dollars ($1,000) and not more than five thousand dollars ($5,000), or imprisonment not exceeding one year in the county jail, or both the fine and imprisonment in the discretion of the court."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax Code § 7153, California Sales and Use Tax Law, Chapter 10 (Violations), general misdemeanor penalty (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=7153.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own criminal penalty for unlicensed selling — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific person's conduct, and not a claim that other states attach the same penalty, or any penalty, to comparable conduct. This clause cites two different statutory sections, not subsections of one section: Cal. Rev. & Tax Code § 6071 defines the misdemeanor and states that its punishment is as provided in a separate section, and Cal. Rev. & Tax Code § 7153 is that separate section, supplying the actual fine range and imprisonment term; these are treated as two sources on two connected points — the offense and its punishment — not as independent corroboration of the same fact. This information sheet is informational only: it does not determine whether any specific person has engaged in business as a seller without a permit, or what penalty, if any, would apply to any specific person's conduct.

CDTFA'S AUTHORITY TO REQUIRE A SECURITY DEPOSIT
Separately from the permit itself, California's Sales and Use Tax Law gives the state tax agency authority to require a security deposit from a person subject to the law, whenever the agency deems it necessary to ensure compliance; this statute already refers to "the department" by name. Security may be posted as cash, government bonds, or insured bank or savings-and-loan deposits, and is held in trust to be used only as the statute provides. The amount is capped: ordinarily it may not exceed twice a quarterly filer's, or three times a monthly filer's, estimated average tax liability, or $50,000, whichever is less, though a higher cap (three or five times, respectively, or $50,000, whichever is less) applies to a person who has been given notice of a hearing to show cause why a permit should not be revoked, or whose permit has already been revoked or suspended. Security held by the department is released after a three-year period in which the person has filed all returns and paid all required tax on time, and the department may sell posted security at public auction to recover unpaid tax, with any surplus returned to the person who posted it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The department, whenever it deems it necessary to ensure compliance with this part, may require any person subject thereto, to place with it any security that the department may determine."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax Code § 6701, California Sales and Use Tax Law, Article 1 (Security for Tax), CDTFA's authority to require security (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=6701.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of CDTFA's own security-deposit authority under California's sales and use tax law — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific person's obligations, and not a claim that other states condition an analogous permit or license on a security deposit in the same way or amount. This clause cites a single statutory section, Cal. Rev. & Tax Code § 6701, so no same-section multiple-subsection issue arises here. This information sheet is informational only: it does not determine whether the business named in this document or any other specific person would be required to post security, in what amount, or as a condition of what specific permit.

Rather than stating its own fine amount, Section 6071 cross-references Section 7153, the Sales and Use Tax Law's general misdemeanor-penalty provision. Section 7153 states that a violation of the Sales and Use Tax Law, except as otherwise provided, is a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of not less than $1,000 and not more than $5,000, or by imprisonment not exceeding one year in county jail, or by both the fine and imprisonment, in the court's discretion.

Security may be posted as cash, government bonds, or insured bank or savings-and-loan deposits, and is held in trust to be used only as the statute provides. The amount is capped: ordinarily it may not exceed twice a quarterly filer's, or three times a monthly filer's, estimated average tax liability, or $50,000, whichever is less, though a higher cap (three or five times, respectively, or $50,000, whichever is less) applies to a person who has been given notice of a hearing to show cause why a permit should not be revoked, or whose permit has already been revoked or suspended. Security held by the department is released after a three-year period in which the person has filed all returns and paid all required tax on time, and the department may sell posted security at public auction to recover unpaid tax, with any surplus returned to the person who posted it.
